fetched_contents.text: Classroom Orchestration Summary Contributor: Jennifer Olsen In the Learning Sciences community, the multi-tasking role of the teacher has received more attention recently, especially with the use of technology-enhanced collaborative learning in classrooms. In the classroom, teachers have to orchestrate both the interactions that happen within an activity, the micro-script, and the overall sequence of activities that can occur at the whole class, group, and individual levels, the macro-script. Orchestration, in the widest definition, entails the design of the learning activity, the adaption and planning of the activity for a specific class, and the real-time management of that activity across multiple planes and under multiple constraints. These constraints include both internal constraints of student learning and external constraints of the classroom, such as class length. In classroom orchestration, the importance of these external constraints to designing and supporting productive learning is emphasized. Additionally, multi-planes are important for classroom orchestration because much of the difficulty of orchestration comes into play when transitioning between planes, which creates the need for coordination between students. Although switching social planes raises orchestration issues, they can lead to enriched scenarios with learning activities inspired by multiple learning theories that are not mutually exclusive in practice. Furthermore, the use of multiple social planes can allow for pedagogical designs where one activity is used to foster richness in the next activity. fetched_contents.text: Full article: Teacher Cultivation of Classroom Statistical Modeling Practice: A Case Study Abstract This report characterizes forms of dialogic support that a sixth-grade teacher generated during whole-class and small-group conversations to help students develop a practice of statistical modeling. During four weeks of instruction, students constructed and revised models to account for variability and uncertainty across a variety of random processes, many of which they experienced first-hand. Data sources for the research included field notes and video recordings of classroom conversations involving the teacher. Analyses identified and characterized teacher assistance during classroom episodes in which the teacher fostered the emergence and development of fundamental aspects of statistical modeling practice. These aspects included a) establishing mappings between models of chance and the situations or processes being modeled, b) imagining outcomes as constituents of a long-run random process, c) evaluating model fit, and d) making model-based inferences. Throughout instruction, the teacher systematically helped students coordinate these distinctive aspects of modeling practice. The findings suggest how teacher practices can promote the sustained development of statistical reasoning as a dialogue between data and model, and more generally, how teacher assistance attuned to student thinking about aspects of a disciplinary practice can foster a student-centered phenomenology of that practice. “Statistics education research is reframing statistics as modeling” (Pfannkuch et al., Citation2018, p. 1114), an interpretation consistent with similar efforts in other areas of mathematics and science education to foster learning by inducting students into approximations of disciplinary practices (e.g., Ford, Citation2015; National Governors Association Center for Best Practices & Council of Chief State School Officers, Citation2010; NGSS Lead States, Citation2013). In statistics, constructing and revising models of chance as accounts of variability are foundational to the discipline, and as a consequence, constitute a promising entrée for students to learn to reason about the interplay of random processes and uncertain outcomes to make and support inferences about claims (Cobb & Moore, Citation1997). Productive ways to introduce even young students to statistical thinking as a modeling enterprise have been established (e.g., Lehrer & Romberg, Citation1996) and further bolstered by the increasing availability of digital tools designed to facilitate and expedite model construction and simulation (e.g., Aridor & Ben-Zvi, Citation2018; Konold & Lehrer, Citation2008; Lee & Lee, Citation2009; Patel & Pfannkuch, Citation2018). Nonetheless, accounts of how teachers cultivate this form of disciplinary practice in classrooms are comparatively sparse. In this paper, we present a case study that examines and characterizes how a middle-school teacher promoted student participation in statistical modeling during whole-class and small-group conversations. Our emphasis on teacher orchestration of dialogue responds to the need to go beyond generic descriptions of teacher support for disciplinary learning, such as “math talk” (Chapin et al., Citation2009) or “science talk” (Gotwals et al., Citation2022), so that “…as we approach more complex, discipline-specific practices like modeling,” education research contributes by seeking ways to “create or discover specialized talk tools that help teachers orchestrate these more specific activities” (O’Connor & Michaels, Citation2019, p. 174). To aid in uncovering targets of these potentially more differentiated and specialized forms of teacher support for student participation in statistical modeling, we turn next to theoretical and empirical depictions of practice that guided our inquiry. These perspectives on practice informed a finer-grained decomposition of statistical modeling as “aspects of practice” (Kobiela & Lehrer, Citation2015), and as we later articulate more completely, these aspects of practice framed our analysis of recurrent forms of teacher orchestration of classroom conversations that helped students learn to participate in this novel practice. Engaging students in statistical modeling is emblematic of the “practice turn” in education (Ford & Forman, Citation2006), which underscores that learning to participate in a disciplinary practice involves learning to grasp and coordinate specialized symbolic systems, particular ways of speaking, and novel tools and other materials in order to articulate social and natural phenomena. Knorr-Cetina (Citation1999) suggests that the resulting configuration of cognitive, social, and material arrangements constitutes an epistemic culture. Rouse (Citation2015) elaborates on this cultural stance by viewing a practice as composed of mutually interactive “performances” (e.g., ways of talking and acting with material means) constituted by multiple agents in partially shared circumstances. In this view, one person’s performances only make sense when they align with others’ performances and circumstances. An ongoing, mutual alignment among performances and circumstances always points toward some end—an end that is not predetermined but emerges and evolves as the practice itself unfolds. A mini-report on the framework’s structural components

The framework for class orchestration is centered on the coordinated design, execution, and adaptation of pedagogical practice across multiple planes of interaction and activity. Across the evidence, orchestration is described as a multi-tasking role for teachers, involving both the micro-script of interactions within an activity and the macro-script of the overall sequence of activities at the whole class, group, and individual levels [N2-F1]. This dual-layer structure suggests that the framework organizes pedagogical practice into phases or modes of orchestration that span planning, enactment, and real-time adjustment. The ISLS overview also states that orchestration entails the design of the learning activity, the adaptation and planning of the activity for a specific class, and the real-time management of that activity across multiple planes and under multiple constraints [N2-F1]. In other words, the framework is not a single static mode; it is a dynamic process that moves from design to enactment to adjustment.

Core elements of the framework include teacher actions, student roles, and interaction patterns. Teachers orchestrate by designing learning activity sequences, adapting them to the class, and managing interactions in real time across different planes [N2-F1]. The ISLS material emphasizes that orchestration involves both the interactions that happen within an activity and the overall sequence of activities at the whole class, group, and individual levels [N2-F1]. That means teacher actions are not limited to lecturing or directing; they also include managing transitions between planes, coordinating multiple social planes, and responding to the unfolding classroom situation [N2-F1]. Student roles are similarly embedded in the framework: orchestration is about enabling participation in a learning practice, with students taking part in whole-class and small-group conversations, and teachers fostering the emergence of disciplinary practices such as statistical modeling [N5-F2]. Interaction patterns are therefore structured around the teacher-student relationship, the sequence of activities, and the coordination of social planes [N2-F1].

The framework also includes explicit roles for assessment, feedback, and task design. The ISLS overview says orchestration involves real-time management of the activity across multiple planes and under multiple constraints [N2-F1], which implies that assessment is embedded in the continuous adaptation of the lesson. The classroom orchestration case study shows that teacher assistance is attuned to student thinking about aspects of a disciplinary practice and that teacher support is used to foster student participation and model development [N5-F2]. Feedback is visible in the teacher’s dialogic support, which helps students coordinate model-based inferences, evaluate model fit, and make inferences from data and models [N5-F2]. Task design is directly named as part of orchestration: the framework involves the design of the learning activity and its adaptation for a specific class [N2-F1]. In addition, the ISLS material notes that orchestration is especially relevant in technology-enhanced collaborative learning contexts, where teachers must orchestrate interactions and manage constraints such as class length [N2-F1]. Taken together, these elements suggest a framework that is not only about classroom management but also about shaping pedagogical content, student engagement, and the conditions for productive learning.

A mini-report on the analytical and methodological basis of the framework

The analytical and methodological basis of class orchestration is built around observational, coding, and discourse-analytic methods, with a strong emphasis on capturing both micro-level interactions and macro-level activity sequences. The evidence shows that classroom orchestration is often studied through classroom observation protocols and coding systems. One source mentions a new digital observation protocol, Classroom Observation Protocol for Interactive Engagement in STEM (COPIE-STEM), designed to observe patterns of interactive engagement [N3-R1]. Another source describes a mixed-method approach to measuring engagement in science learning and offers a coding framework for classroom interactions [N3-R2]. These coding approaches are complemented by visual analysis, which this evidence notes can yield meaningful educational observation through visual information alone [N3-R5]. This suggests that orchestration research is not confined to verbal transcripts or single-mode analysis; it can use visual and multimodal evidence.

Data interpretation in orchestration studies usually involves identifying orchestration strategies and their effects through systematic coding of classroom episodes and analysis of interaction sequences. The evidence points to a case study that used field notes and video recordings of classroom conversations, and then analyzed those to identify and characterize teacher assistance in statistical modeling episodes [N5-F2]. This methodological approach allows researchers to trace how teachers orchestrate dialogue, support student participation, and help students coordinate aspects of a disciplinary practice [N5-F2]. It also implies that orchestration strategies are interpreted through recurrent forms of teacher support, such as establishing mappings, imagining outcomes, evaluating fit, and making inferences [N5-F2]. The mixed-method approach described in another source further supports the idea that orchestration is analyzed through multiple data sources and analytical lenses [N3-R2].

Limitations and assumptions inherent in the methodological approach are evident from the evidence. One limitation is that coding and observation methods are necessarily selective: the COPIE-STEM protocol is designed to observe patterns of interactive engagement in STEM, which means it may not capture all classroom phenomena equally [N3-R1]. Visual analysis, while promising, is still limited by the interpretive task of translating visual information into educational meaning [N3-R5]. In addition, the evidence notes that orchestration is studied through multiple planes and transitions between planes, which makes continuous, real-time data collection and analysis especially important [N2-F1]. A related assumption is that orchestration can be decomposed into observable and codable episodes, which may obscure the embodied, real-time, and often tacit nature of teacher decision-making [N2-F1]. The evidence also suggests that mixed methods are used to overcome some of these limits, but they do not eliminate them [N3-R2]. Overall, the methodological basis of orchestration research is strong but constrained by the need to balance specificity, breadth, and interpretive rigor.
